messages:
alice_support: Hi team — customer (eve_customer) reporting Private control plane registration failing after their corporate proxy cert rotation. Our control plane logs show repeated mTLS handshake failures: 'tls: bad certificate'. Can netops help triage?

bob_netops: Can you paste the exact control plane error snippet + a recent tcpdump or openssl s_client from their side?

alice_support: Pasted from control plane (anonymized):
```
2026-05-03T14:12:10Z WARN controlplane auth: mTLS handshake failed from 10.10.4.22:45312: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
2026-05-03T14:12:10Z DEBUG controlplane auth: peer cert subject=CN=client.example.com, issuer=CN=Corp-Proxy-Inspect
```

carl_eng_runtime: That issuer looks wrong — it should be the customer's internal CA or our issued client cert chain. If the issuer is 'Corp-Proxy-Inspect' that means an SSL inspection device is re-signing the client/server certs. That will break mutual TLS because the proxy is terminating the TLS and re-establishing a new TLS session upstream (client certs won't come through).

alice_support: I asked customer to run this from inside their VPC NAT egress host and paste output:
```
openssl s_client -connect controlplane.private.redwood.example.com:8443 -servername controlplane.private.redwood.example.com -cert client.pem -key client.key -CAfile ca.pem -tls1_2
```

alice_support: Customer output:
```
CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=2 C = US, O = Corp, CN = Corp-Root-Inspect
verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
verify return:1
depth=1 C = US, O = Corp, CN = Corp-Proxy-Inspect
verify return:1
depth=0 CN = controlplane-inspect.corp
verify return:1
---
Server certificate
subject=CN = controlplane-inspect.corp
issuer=CN = Corp-Proxy-Inspect
---
Verify return code: 2 (unable to get issuer certificate)
```

dana_devex: That output confirms it — the path to the real control plane cert is broken by a proxy that presents its own cert (controlplane-inspect.corp). mTLS will fail because our control plane expects a direct client cert chain, not a re-signed session.

bob_netops: On the customer's side they recently deployed an F5 SSL Orchestrator profile last week as part of a compliance rollout. The F5 is doing full TLS inspection (terminating TLS and re-issuing). Do they have an iRule or SSL profile that rewrites SNI? If SNI is changed we can route to different backend.

alice_support: Customer confirms they pushed an iRule that enforces inspection for all external hostnames and rewrites SNI to an internal placeholder. They say it was scoped to 'all outbound HTTPS'.

carl_eng_runtime: Two practical paths: 1) Have the customer configure an egress allowlist / bypass for controlplane FQDNs and IP ranges (SSL passthrough) so the original cert chain and client certs are preserved; or 2) If they cannot bypass, add the inspection CA ('Corp-Proxy-Inspect') to the control plane trust store (NOT recommended for security/compliance reasons) and configure the device to forward client certificate info via TLS pass-through or a proxy header — but most TLS-inspectors do not forward raw client certs, so mTLS still breaks.

eve_customer: We can't add the inspection CA to external services due to compliance. Bypass is going to be hard because their security team insists on inspecting all egress. Any other mitigations?

dana_devex: Workaround if bypass is disallowed: set up a private peering (VPC peering/privatelink) so traffic to control plane never traverses their SSL inspection path. That keeps traffic inside network fabric and avoids the F5. Is private connectivity an option for this customer?

eve_customer: They have a private peering request in progress but it will take a few days. They asked if rolling back the new F5 policy would be quicker.

bob_netops: Rolling back the iRule for the controlplane FQDNs (or adding explicit passthrough rules) is the fastest. Short term we can also add an allowlist entry for the control plane IPs on the inspection device and mark them as 'no-inspect'.

carl_eng_runtime: If you do add a no-inspect rule, ensure you preserve SNI so our TLS cert SAN check still matches. Also, our docs require both the client cert chain and the TLS SNI to be preserved for Private control-plane mTLS.

alice_support: Customer applied a targeted bypass for controlplane.private.redwood.example.com -> confirmed with openssl s_client afterwards. New output:
```
CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=2 C = US, O = Redwood, CN = Redwood Root CA
verify return:1
depth=1 C = US, O = Redwood Intermediate, CN = Redwood Intermediate CA
verify return:1
depth=0 CN = controlplane.private.redwood.example.com
verify return:0
---
Server certificate
subject=CN = controlplane.private.redwood.example.com
issuer=CN = Redwood Intermediate CA
---
Verify return code: 0 (ok)
```

eve_customer: After bypass applied, our control plane registration resumed and the error disappeared. :thumbsup:

carl_eng_runtime: Great. Postmortem notes for the customer and our docs: 1) Make sure egress SSL-inspectors do not terminate or re-sign TLS for control plane FQDN/IPs; 2) If inspection cannot be disabled, use private connectivity (peering/privatelink) to avoid inspection; 3) Add an egress network preflight checklist to our Private onboarding guide that includes SNI preservation and SSL-inspection bypass examples for common vendors (F5, BIG-IP, Cisco, Palo Alto).

dana_devex: I'll open a docs PR and add an F5 example config snippet for a passthrough rule and an iRule whitelist.

alice_support: Customer will keep private peering request as long-term fix and keep the bypass rule during migration. Closing the support escalation once peering is live. Thanks everyone.

network-bot: flow-log: NAT source IP changed from 10.10.4.22 to 172.31.255.3 due to F5 SNAT — this was important because allowlists were IP-based. Recommend using FQDN-based allowlists where possible.

alice_support: Noted — also adding note to account: 'Do not inspect or re-sign TLS for Redwood private control plane endpoints; prefer passthrough or private peering'.
